clinicalPearls: Retrograde flow of urine from the bladder into the ureter and sometimes the renal pelvis, which may be primary (congenital incompetence of the ureterovesical junction) or secondary to raised bladder pressure or outlet obstruction
Graded I to V on micturating cystourethrogram, from reflux into a non-dilated ureter (grade I) to gross dilatation and tortuosity with loss of papillary detail (grade V)
Often detected during evaluation of antenatal hydronephrosis or after a febrile urinary tract infection in a child
The main long-term concern is reflux nephropathy: renal scarring that can lead to hypertension, proteinuria, and chronic kidney disease, particularly when reflux and infection coexist
Lower grades frequently resolve spontaneously with growth as the intramural ureter lengthens
Bladder and bowel dysfunction strongly influences persistence, infection risk, and treatment success and should be actively addressed
Management options include surveillance, continuous antibiotic prophylaxis, and, for higher grades or breakthrough infections, ureteric reimplantation or endoscopic injection
reference.pathophysiology: The normal ureterovesical junction acts as a one-way flap valve because the intravesical ureter runs obliquely through the bladder wall and is compressed during filling and voiding. In primary reflux this valve is incompetent, usually because of a short intramural ureteric tunnel or a laterally placed ureteric orifice. Secondary reflux develops when abnormally high bladder pressures, as in outlet obstruction or neurogenic or dysfunctional bladders, overwhelm a marginally competent junction. Reflux of infected urine, and possibly of sterile urine at high pressure, delivers pathogens and pressure to the renal papillae, producing pyelonephritic inflammation and scarring known as reflux nephropathy.
additionalDifferentials: Duplex collecting system with a refluxing lower moiety
Simple recurrent lower urinary tract infection without reflux
additionalInvestigations: Micturating cystourethrogram (MCUG) to confirm and grade reflux
Renal and bladder ultrasound to assess dilatation, scarring, and bladder wall
DMSA scintigraphy to detect renal scarring and differential function
Assessment of bladder and bowel function, including a voiding diary
Urinalysis and culture during suspected infection
Blood pressure measurement and renal function tests during follow-up
redFlags: Breakthrough febrile urinary tract infections despite prophylaxis
New or progressive renal scarring on serial imaging
Hypertension or proteinuria indicating reflux nephropathy
Bilateral high-grade reflux with declining renal function
reference.prognosis: Low-grade reflux commonly resolves spontaneously with an excellent prognosis, whereas high-grade bilateral reflux, especially with recurrent pyelonephritis and pre-existing dysplasia, carries a meaningful risk of scarring, hypertension, and chronic kidney disease requiring long-term monitoring.
pitfalls: Attributing all renal damage to reflux when congenital dysplasia may account for much of it
Ignoring underlying bladder and bowel dysfunction, which undermines both medical and surgical treatment
Over-investigating or over-treating low-grade reflux likely to resolve spontaneously
Failing to monitor blood pressure and renal function in children with established scarring
